projects.overview: CASH-G is an educational banking simulator built in two distinct versions. Desktop v1 uses Java Swing, JDBC, and PostgreSQL. Web v2 is a separate Spring Boot and Thymeleaf application with a local H2 practice demo. The repositories retain earlier names—JCash for the desktop repository and Cash - G for the web repository—while this portfolio uses CASH-G consistently.

architecture.summary: These versions share a project history, not an interface or one deployment path.

workflow: Desktop v1 supports account registration and sign-in, cash-in, transfers, and per-user transaction history.
Web v2 presents multiple synthetic practice accounts and a review step before a transfer.
The local web demo also includes requests, fictional billers, savings goals, cards, activity, and statement export.
The screenshots on this page show the web v2 interface only; an authentic desktop v1 screenshot was not available for this portfolio update.

decisions.title: Keep both sides of a transfer together
decisions.body: The Java persistence layer records the sender debit, recipient credit, and paired ledger entries in a bounded database transaction. Its documented behavior rolls the operation back when a step fails.

decisions.title: Represent money deliberately
decisions.body: Java monetary values use BigDecimal and database numeric columns. The web version keeps the review step on the server before confirmation.

decisions.title: Separate interface, rules, and persistence
decisions.body: Swing or web controllers handle interaction, Java services own product rules, and JDBC repositories perform database work. The version-specific code and tests are linked below.

projects.overview: ARCTIC models service operations for a four-branch air-conditioning company. It connects customer requests and dispatch to service jobs, equipment and parts, invoices, receipts, and branch-filtered reporting.

architecture.summary: The interface supports branch workflows; the API applies organization and branch checks before data access.

accessModel.summary: These are the application's two account roles. A technician is an assignee, not a third sign-in role; technician and booking must share a branch.

roles.name: BRANCH_LEADER
roles.scope: Reads and writes stay within the user's assigned branch.

workflow: Staff record service requests for a customer, site, branch, and unit.
A job is scheduled and assigned to a technician in its branch.
The work order records inspection outcomes before completion.
An invoice follows completed work; collections and receipts are recorded separately.
Managers review jobs, stock, maintenance, and balances by branch.

decisions.title: Make job progression explicit
decisions.body: A shared transition map permits the documented job states in order. Completed and cancelled jobs are terminal through the ordinary status flow, so a normal edit cannot silently reopen work.

decisions.title: Enforce organization and branch boundaries
decisions.body: Server-side queries and writes check the organization, branch, and related records. The workflow does not rely on the interface alone to hide another branch’s data.

decisions.title: Keep payment history auditable
decisions.body: Amounts use fixed-precision decimal fields. Payment moves through unpaid, partial, and paid states; a refund requires its own recorded workflow rather than resetting a paid invoice.

sourceEvidence.label: Branch access rules
sourceEvidence.detail: Server helpers used for organization, branch, unit, customer, and technician scope.

sourceEvidence.label: Booking status tests
sourceEvidence.detail: Focused checks for the service-job lifecycle.

projects.role: I handled requirements gathering, workflow definition, data-architecture decisions, and deployment work. Implementation was AI-assisted.
projects.verificationSummary: The published record reports 29 unit tests passed, 12 database tests skipped in that mode, and 41 integration tests passed against an isolated PostgreSQL database. It also documents the production migration and smoke checks; no production user account was used.
projects.portfolioCheck: On October 8, the local synthetic demo was opened through its demo-workspace control. I captured the dashboard, service-jobs list, and invoices view without editing records. The separate public check confirmed sign-in and health only; no hosted authenticated workflow was exercised.
projects.applicationNote: The public application opens at its sign-in page. This portfolio update did not verify an authenticated hosted session.
limitations: The four-branch company is a modeled scenario; no production adoption or business-impact figures are claimed.
The local gallery uses synthetic demo records.

projects.overview: AssetHub is a multi-tenant equipment workspace. It tracks equipment custody and location across organization workspaces, with checkout and return, location transfers, maintenance, audits, invitations, permissions, and retirement that preserves history.

architecture.summary: Workspace membership and role checks happen on the server before tenant-scoped records are read or changed.

accessModel.summary: Authentication identifies the user; an active membership is checked for the selected organization on protected requests. Choosing an organization alone does not grant access.

roles.name: MANAGER
roles.scope: Manages inventory, locations, categories, maintenance, and audits.

roles.name: MEMBER
roles.scope: Views workspace assets and reports issues.

workflow: Workspace members add equipment with its location and identifying details.
A checkout records the custodian and expected return.
Returned equipment, location changes, and maintenance remain in its history.
Location audits compare a fixed snapshot and reject stale updates.
Retired assets remain recorded rather than disappearing from the workspace.

decisions.title: Scope every workspace operation
decisions.body: Organization membership is checked on server requests, and tenant-specific relationships constrain records. Reads and writes use workspace scope rather than relying on client-side filtering.

decisions.title: Protect concurrent custody changes
decisions.body: A database constraint allows only one open checkout per asset. Asset transitions and activity history are committed together.

decisions.title: Preserve history through the lifecycle
decisions.body: Assets retire instead of being deleted. Version checks reject stale audit updates so a saved audit does not silently overwrite newer state.

sourceEvidence.label: Organization membership middleware
sourceEvidence.detail: Resolves an active membership before protected workspace operations.

sourceEvidence.label: Tenant and lifecycle integration tests
sourceEvidence.detail: Includes cross-tenant, member-permission, concurrent-checkout, and lifecycle checks.

projects.role: I built an earlier multi-tenant asset manager on my own. In 2026, I rebuilt and expanded it with AI assistance—refining the interface, fixing issues, and adding lifecycle and workspace features. This page describes the current rebuild.
projects.verificationSummary: The published record includes tenant and permission checks, concurrent checkout, return and maintenance transitions, versioned audits, isolated demo workspaces, browser checks, and deployment verification. Its fixtures are synthetic; the record does not authenticate as an original user.
projects.portfolioCheck: On October 8, the independent public check confirmed the sign-in page and health response only; no authenticated hosted session was created. The gallery uses genuine screenshots published in the project repository.
projects.applicationNote: The hosted application opens at sign-in. The published verification record covers authenticated flows; this portfolio update did not repeat them.
limitations: AssetHub is an educational portfolio project; no customer adoption or business outcome is claimed.
Invitations are copyable links; the application does not send email.
